items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: I play Ahmad Jamal, Gene Harris, or Zoot, or Zoot and Al, or Dizzy, or Miles. You know, all those, Hawk. Good stuff.

ctx.x: What do you listen to at home these days? Anything in particular?

You know it’s very funny because I love talk radio, because it’s immediate. And I love things like Jeopardy on television. I learn a lot from that, and when I play music I play Ahmad Jamal, Gene Harris, or Zoot, or Zoot and Al, or Dizzy, or Miles. You know, all those, Hawk. Good stuff. As well as South American things.
Do you have vocalists that you still love that you listened to on the way up, and who were they?

items.title: Annie Ross — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I remember when I was living in Paris in this hotel, I went to North Africa with Hawk [Coleman Hawkins] and Klook and Moody.

ctx.x: He was born on Christmas Eve. Was it 1950? His full name was Kenneth Christopher Clarke, Christopher being one of Charlie Parker’s names. Bird sent a telegram saying, “I still got lots of other names left.” When I came from Pittsburgh with my child, we went and stayed with Bird, who was with Chan and Pree, the little girl who died. We all packed into this apartment. It was quite wonderful. There were a lot of kids. It was a lot of noise. Again, we had no money. Bird came home with a ham. Boy, a ham. I prepared it…

Klook had impressed on me, time. So when I would get together with he and Moody, it was all about ears. Even when I was in Paris, Moody used to come with Ravel or Debussy. He’d say, listen to that thing that Debussy does [Ross sings], and I could hear the chord change. So Moody was responsible for my enlarging my capacity to hear. It was a fantastic schooling.
